blocks.text: 1. Multi-Hop Retrieval
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443923-730248731.png
Multi-Hop Retrieval introduces sequential dependency between retrieval steps: retrieval chains across multiple reasoning steps, with each step building on what the previous one found.
It uses the results of one retrieval step to shape the next retrieval step, a chained retrieval strategy.
2. From Parallel Variations To Sequential Steps
Multi-Query Retrieval ran several variations of a query in parallel, independently, searching each variation separately.
Multi-hop retrieval instead runs retrieval steps in sequence, each depending on the last.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Technique","Step relationship"],"rows":[["Multi-query retrieval","Parallel, independent variations"],["Multi-hop retrieval","Sequential, each step depends on the last"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Questions That Need Multiple Facts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443923-922008651.png
As with decomposition into subqueries in Query Transformation, some questions require combining facts found in separate chunks.
A single retrieval pass cannot connect information that never appears together in the same chunk.
4. The First Hop Finds A Partial Answer

blocks.alt: The First Hop Finds A Partial Answer
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443923-52951498.png
The first retrieval step searches with the original question and finds a partial answer or a needed intermediate fact.
That partial answer becomes an ingredient for the next step, not the final answer itself.
5. Using The First Hop To Form The Second Query

blocks.alt: Using The First Hop To Form The Second Query
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443924-733798188.png
As with rewriting with an LLM in Query Rewriting, the intermediate fact gets used to build a new, more specific follow-up query.
That second query searches for what the first hop's answer still left unresolved.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A question like "who founded the company that makes this product" needs a first hop to identify the company, then a second hop using that company name to find its founder.

blocks.text: 6. Chaining As Many Hops As Needed

blocks.alt: Chaining As Many Hops As Needed
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447443924-59080687.png
Some questions need three, four, or more chained retrieval steps before reaching a complete answer.
Each additional hop narrows or extends what the previous hops already established.
7. Knowing When To Stop Hopping
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447444328-421403274.png
A system needs some way to decide that the chain of retrievals is actually complete.
Stopping too early leaves the answer incomplete; stopping too late wastes retrieval effort.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A common stopping rule checks whether the accumulated information from all hops so far already answers the original question, halting the chain as soon as that check succeeds.

blocks.text: 8. Cost And Latency Of Chained Retrieval
As with the multiplied retrieval cost in Multi-Query Retrieval, each additional hop adds its own retrieval and reasoning latency.
A multi-hop chain can take noticeably longer than a single retrieval pass.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Number of hops","Typical latency impact"],"rows":[["One hop, a normal retrieval pass","Baseline latency"],["Multiple chained hops","Latency grows with each sequential step"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Multi-Hop Retrieval Is Necessary

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Multi-Hop Retrieval Is Necessary
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447444330-457712659.png
Questions requiring connected facts across separate sources need multi-hop retrieval.
Questions answerable from a single chunk never need the extra hops at all.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates chaining two retrieval hops to answer a question requiring connected facts.

code.content:
documents = {
    "d1": "The Aurora Project was developed by Skylark Labs.",
    "d2": "Skylark Labs was founded by Maya Chen in 2018.",
    "d3": "The weather today is sunny with a light breeze.",
}

def fake_search(query_terms, documents):
    for doc_id, text in documents.items():
        if all(term.lower() in text.lower() for term in query_terms):
            return doc_id, text
    return None, None

question = "Who founded the company behind the Aurora Project"

print(f"Question: {question!r}\n")

# First hop: find the company behind the Aurora Project
hop1_id, hop1_text = fake_search(["Aurora Project"], documents)
print(f"Hop 1 result: {hop1_id} -> {hop1_text!r}")

# Second hop: use the company name to find its founder
company_name = "Skylark Labs"
hop2_id, hop2_text = fake_search([company_name, "founded"], documents)
print(f"Hop 2 result: {hop2_id} -> {hop2_text!r}")

print(f"\nFinal answer assembled from both hops:")
print(f"  The Aurora Project's company, {company_name}, was founded as described in hop 2.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the first hop identifying the company, and the second hop using that company name to find the founder, connecting facts no single retrieval pass would have found.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using a single retrieval pass for a question that requires connecting facts across sources.
Chaining hops indefinitely without a clear stopping rule for when the answer is complete.
Ignoring the added latency cost that each additional hop introduces to a multi-hop chain.
Applying multi-hop retrieval to simple questions answerable from a single chunk.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Multi-hop retrieval uses the results of one retrieval step to shape the next retrieval step.
Unlike multi-query retrieval's parallel variations, multi-hop retrieval runs sequential, dependent steps.
Some questions require combining facts found in separate chunks that no single pass can connect.
The first hop searches with the original question and finds a partial answer or intermediate fact.
That intermediate fact gets used to build a new, more specific follow up query.
Some questions need three or more chained hops before reaching a complete answer.
A system needs a clear rule to decide when the chain of retrievals is actually complete.
Each additional hop adds real retrieval and reasoning latency to the overall chain.
